name: Olanzapine
sections: Yellow crystalline solid; melting point 195 °C; practically insoluble in water.

Discovered while searching for a clozapine analogue that would not require routine blood monitoring, resulting in a thienobenzodiazepine structure. First approval/introduction: US FDA 1996 (Eli Lilly and Company); patented 1991.

Antagonist at dopamine D1–D4, serotonin 5-HT2A/2C, muscarinic M1–M5, histamine H1 and alpha-1 adrenergic receptors. Greater 5-HT2 than D2 blockade gives antipsychotic and mood-stabilising effects with low EPS liability. Receptor / target profile: Higher affinity for 5-HT2A (Ki 1.3–24 nM) than D2 (Ki 3–106 nM); antagonism at H1, muscarinic and alpha-1 receptors contributes to sedation and weight gain.
Hepatic – direct glucuronidation and CYP1A2-mediated oxidation
Summary: Well absorbed; Tmax 5–8 h, unaffected by food. ~93% protein bound. Metabolised by CYP1A2 and glucuronidation. Half-life 21–54 h (shorter in smokers).
Moderate-to-severe manic episodes of bipolar disorder
Prevention of recurrence in bipolar disorder (responders)
Schizophrenia: start 10 mg once daily; range 5–20 mg/day
Mania: 15 mg once daily (10 mg in combination therapy); range 5–20 mg/day
Elderly, hepatic impairment, female non-smokers: consider starting 5 mg
MD tablet: place on tongue to disperse, or dissolve in water/juice; with or without food
Dose to be individualised by the treating physician according to clinical response and tolerability.
Moderate impairment: start 5 mg; increase cautiously.
Start 2.5–5 mg; increased mortality with dementia; risk of falls and orthostasis.
Adolescents (13–17 y): greater weight gain and lipid changes; consider other agents first.
Use only if benefit justifies risk; neonatal EPS/withdrawal after third-trimester exposure.
Excreted in breast milk; breastfeeding not recommended.
Significant weight gain, hyperglycaemia/diabetes and dyslipidaemia – monitor metabolic parameters
Increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia
Anticholinergic effects – caution in prostatic hypertrophy, paralytic ileus
Orthostatic hypotension; transient raised liver enzymes
Raised prolactin, glucose, triglycerides and cholesterol
Smoking and carbamazepine induce CYP1A2 (lower levels)
Fluvoxamine and ciprofloxacin inhibit CYP1A2 (raise levels)
With or without food; smoking induces metabolism (dose changes needed on stopping smoking); avoid alcohol.
Weight monthly for 3 months then quarterly; fasting glucose and lipids at baseline, 3 months, then annually; LFTs; CBC if neutropenia risk.
Tachycardia, agitation, dysarthria, EPS, reduced consciousness, rarely delirium or NMS-like picture. Supportive care; activated charcoal; avoid adrenaline for hypotension.
CATIE (Lieberman et al., NEJM 2005) – olanzapine had the longest time to all-cause discontinuation but the greatest weight gain and metabolic changes.
Leucht et al., Lancet 2013 – among the most efficacious antipsychotics.
Expect increased appetite – follow diet and exercise plan
May cause drowsiness – avoid driving initially
Tell your doctor if you stop or start smoking
Store below 30°C in a dry place, protected from light and moisture. Keep out of the reach of children. Do not use after the expiry date.
